title: How stars end
intro_sentence: A star's mass decides its death. Stars up to about eight times the Sun's shed their outer layers and leave a white dwarf; heavier ones usually explode, leaving a neutron star or a black hole.
body_paragraphs: A star with less than about eight times the Sun's mass ends quietly. When the hydrogen in its core runs out, fusion moves to the outer layers, which expand, and the star becomes a red giant. Eventually the star becomes unstable and blows its outer layers away as an expanding cloud of gas and dust, a planetary nebula. The name has nothing to do with planets: it comes from their round, planet-like look in small telescopes. What lights the cloud is the exposed core, which is hot enough (above about 30,000 kelvin) to ionise the gas with its ultraviolet light. The glow lasts only of the order of ten thousand years, a short phase in a star's life.

What is left at the centre is a white dwarf: the core, no longer fusing anything, slowly cooling. A typical one has about half the Sun's mass in a body only slightly bigger than Earth. Its electrons, packed as tightly as quantum physics allows, hold it up. This has a ceiling: Subrahmanyan Chandrasekhar showed that a white dwarf cannot exceed about 1.4 solar masses. Two planetary nebulae to look at are the Ring Nebula (M57), about 2,570 light-years away, where Hubble found a football-shaped structure seen end-on piercing the ring, and the Dumbbell Nebula (M27), about 1,270 light-years away, the first planetary nebula ever discovered, by Charles Messier in 1764.

Stars above about eight solar masses end in a collapse that is usually a supernova. When fusion can no longer support the core, it collapses and rebounds, sending a shock wave through the star. In 1054 Chinese astronomers recorded a guest star that, according to their records, stayed visible in daylight for 23 days; its remnant is the Crab Nebula (M1), now about six light-years wide and about 6,520 light-years away. Cassiopeia A, about 11,000 light-years away, is another remnant, from an explosion whose light reached Earth in the late 17th century. NASA gives roughly eight to 20 solar masses as the range of stars that leave neutron stars; heavier stars leave black holes.

The core of the Crab is a neutron star, between about one and three solar masses squeezed into a ball about 20 kilometres across, so dense that a sugar cube of it would weigh about a billion tonnes. It spins about 30 times a second, and its beams sweep past Earth like a lighthouse: a pulsar. Pulsars are rotating neutron stars seen as regular pulses, from milliseconds to seconds apart. If the collapsing core is heavier than about three solar masses, nothing stops it, and it keeps collapsing into a stellar-mass black hole. The black holes article covers what happens there.
diagram_caption: Up to ~8 solar masses: red giant, planetary nebula, white dwarf (limit 1.4). Above that: usually a supernova, then a neutron star, or a black hole for the heaviest.
